title: Cartridge, Disposable or All-in-One? | The Bridge
description: Three words for heated oil and a battery. How they differ, why temperature control matters, where to buy, and why a disposable never just goes away.
lede: Three words for one idea: oil, heat and a battery. The real choice is about how much control you want and what happens when it's empty.
html:
Every vape on a menu does the same basic job: it heats a liquid to create an aerosol you inhale, usually with a battery doing the work. What changes is which parts you keep. That one detail decides how much control you get over the heat and what ends up in your trash.

The three words

  • Cartridge. A filled tank of cannabis oil that pairs with a battery you keep. When the oil is gone, the cartridge goes and the battery stays.
  • Disposable. Oil and battery sold as one piece. The FDA's description of vaping products covers this kind: used once and then thrown away.
  • All-in-one. What it says, battery and oil in one body. Don't assume that means it recharges, and don't assume it doesn't. Check the product page or ask.

Heat is the real question

New York's safer consumption guide has a line every vape buyer should read. Some batteries allow hotter temperatures than others, it says, which can potentially release toxic chemicals from the battery and burn off cannabinoids. Its advice is to use suggested cartridge temperatures and avoid batteries that cannot change the temperature.

By the state's own logic, that's an argument for a cartridge on an adjustable battery. If you prefer the convenience of a single device, look for whether it has heat settings at all before you buy.

Small device, strong oil

Size fools people. The state's concentrates brochure says concentrates can range from 50% to 98% THC, against 12% to 30% for typical flower, and recommends them for experienced consumers with a higher tolerance. They can be vaped, and inhaled products come on in about seven to ten minutes. The state's rule of thumb: one or two puffs, then wait five to ten minutes before deciding on more.

Buy it from someone who has to answer for it

This one isn't theoretical. During the lung injury outbreak known as EVALI, the CDC reported 2,807 hospitalized cases or deaths as of February 2020, including 68 confirmed deaths. THC vaping products, particularly from informal sources like friends, family or dealers, were linked to most cases, and vitamin E acetate was strongly linked to the outbreak, though the CDC said other chemicals couldn't be ruled out.

In New York, products sold at licensed dispensaries must pass lab testing, including for pesticides, heavy metals and residual solvents, and the QR code on the label takes you to the results. That doesn't make vaping risk free. The state notes cannabis aerosol can contain harmful chemicals too. It does mean somebody checked.

Respect the battery

The FDA's vape battery tips are simple. Follow the manufacturer's directions. Use only batteries recommended for your device. Charge on a clean, flat surface where you can see it, not on a couch or pillow. Keep it out of direct sun and out of a hot car.

A disposable doesn't disappear

The word is misleading. The EPA says lithium-ion batteries and devices containing them should not go in household garbage or recycling bins, because they can get crushed and start fires. Its e-cigarette tip sheet adds that you should not try to pry out batteries that aren't designed to come out, and that each device should go in its own plastic bag. Household hazardous waste collection is the place for it, and your local sanitation agency can tell you where. That guidance was written for nicotine devices. A lithium battery is a lithium battery.

So which one?

New to this: buy the smallest thing that does the job, and go slow. Regular user: a reusable battery with adjustable heat gives you the most control and the least to throw out. Grab and go: an all-in-one is fine, if you've already got a plan for the empty one.
